lessons.title: Comprehension with Transitioning Exercises
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop a wide range of English skills through comprehension, creative writing, grammar, spelling and vocabulary activities.

This lesson includes:
✔ Reading and answering comprehension questions
✔ Retrieving information from fiction and non-fiction texts
✔ Understanding the purpose and effect of a text
✔ Sequencing events in the correct order
✔ Rewriting descriptions using adventurous vocabulary
✔ Using exciting sentence starters
✔ Exploring friendship and relationships through reading
✔ Reading and retrieving information about the history of chocolate
✔ Using conjunctions correctly
✔ Using the past tense
✔ Adding commas to lists
✔ Creating expanded noun phrases
✔ Developing stronger and more interesting vocabulary
✔ Recognising the suffixes -ly and -ful
✔ Practising Year 1 and Year 2 common exception spellings

Students begin with an All About Me activity before improving a jungle description in their own words, using adventurous vocabulary and stronger sentence starters to make the setting vivid and engaging.

The lesson then develops comprehension skills through a timed reading activity about the speed of sound and a series of texts about friendship. Students retrieve information, identify vocabulary in context, sequence events and use evidence from the text to explain their answers.

Students also read about the history of chocolate, answering questions about cacao, the Aztecs, Christopher Columbus, Hernán Cortés, early chocolate houses and the development of chocolate production.

Grammar and vocabulary activities include choosing appropriate conjunctions, working with past tense sentences, punctuating lists with commas, developing expanded noun phrases and replacing ordinary adjectives with more ambitious alternatives.

Students finish by exploring the suffixes -ly and -ful through a hidden-picture activity and correcting twelve misspelt common exception words.

By the end of the lesson, learners will have strengthened their comprehension, grammar, spelling and vocabulary skills while building confidence across a broad range of Year 3 English activities.

lessons.title: Similes and Metaphors
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how similes and metaphors can make writing more vivid, imaginative and powerful. They explore how figurative language creates pictures in the reader’s mind and practise using it to improve their own descriptions.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding what similes are and how they use like or as
✔ Creating similes from pictures and descriptive prompts
✔ Using ambitious adjectives alongside similes
✔ Improving sentences with stronger descriptive language
✔ Understanding metaphors and how they differ from similes
✔ Identifying metaphors in sentences, poetry and prose
✔ Exploring metaphors from The Highwayman by Alfred Noyes
✔ Explaining the effect of figurative language on the reader
✔ Creating metaphors to describe people, body parts and everyday objects
✔ Using animal metaphors to add power and personality
✔ Choosing metaphors to add description, interest and mood
✔ Applying similes and metaphors independently in creative writing

Students begin by exploring familiar similes and creating their own comparisons using like and as. They then combine adjectives and similes to transform simple sentences into more vivid descriptions and develop ambitious vocabulary through descriptive activities.

The lesson then introduces metaphors and examines how direct comparisons differ from similes. Students explore a range of familiar metaphors before studying examples from The Highwayman and discussing how carefully chosen figurative language can create powerful images and atmosphere.

Students develop their own metaphors for people, body parts, objects and animals, considering how each comparison can add description, interest or power to a sentence.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise, explain and create effective similes and metaphors and use them confidently to make their own writing more descriptive, imaginative and engaging.

lessons.title: Present Perfect Tense
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to recognise, form and use the present perfect tense and understand how it differs from the simple past tense.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding when the present perfect tense is used
✔ Recognising the difference between past and present perfect tense
✔ Forming the present perfect tense using has or have
✔ Using past participles correctly
✔ Changing sentences from the past tense to the present perfect tense
✔ Understanding actions that began in the past and continue into the present
✔ Recognising past actions that still have an effect in the present
✔ Choosing correctly between has and have
✔ Working with regular and irregular verbs
✔ Identifying past participles such as grown, done, been and forgotten
✔ Matching past tense verbs with their present perfect forms
✔ Selecting the correct tense according to context and timing
✔ Applying tense knowledge to sentences, recounts and reasoning activities

Students begin by learning how the present perfect tense is formed using has or have with the correct past participle. They practise changing past tense sentences into the present perfect and explore regular and irregular verb forms such as ate and eaten, broke and broken, grew and grown, and did and done.

The lesson then develops students’ understanding of when each tense should be used. They learn that the simple past describes events that started and finished in the past, while the present perfect can describe something that began in the past and continues now or something whose result is still important in the present.

Students practise identifying and correcting verb forms, matching past and present perfect sentences, changing a football recount into the present perfect tense and choosing the correct tense according to the context of a sentence.

Finally, students explore auxiliary verbs and past participles in greater depth, learning when to use has or have and recognising irregular forms such as done, come, forgotten, blown, begun and drawn.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to distinguish between the simple past and present perfect tense, form the present perfect accurately and select the appropriate tense according to meaning and timing.

lessons.title: Articles A, AN & THE
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to choose and use the articles a, an and the correctly, as well as recognising situations where no article is needed.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising vowels and consonants
✔ Choosing between a and an according to the sound of the following word
✔ Understanding why sound rather than spelling determines whether to use a or an
✔ Using a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds
✔ Recognising exceptions such as a unicorn, a university and an hour
✔ Choosing articles when adjectives appear before nouns
✔ Understanding the as the definite article
✔ Using the to refer to a specific person, animal, place or thing
✔ Distinguishing between general and specific references
✔ Recognising situations where no article is required
✔ Using articles correctly with countable and uncountable nouns
✔ Using a or an when introducing something and the when referring to it again
✔ Using articles correctly with rivers, lakes, mountains, mountain ranges, islands and countries
✔ Using the with superlatives
✔ Recognising when institutions such as school and university take no article
✔ Applying article rules accurately within sentences and longer passages

Students begin by revising vowels and consonants before learning the basic rules for a and an. They discover that the sound at the beginning of the following word is more important than its first written letter, explaining why we say a unicorn and a university but an honest person and an hour.

The lesson develops this understanding through sorting, sentence-completion and error-correction activities. Students also explore how adjectives affect the choice of article, comparing examples such as an enormous cat and a delicious egg.

Students then learn about the definite article the and how it identifies a particular person, animal, place or thing. They compare general and specific references and learn how a noun may first be introduced using a or an and then referred to again using the.

The lesson extends into more advanced article rules, including when no article is needed and conventions for geographical names, countries, institutions and superlatives. Students apply these rules to examples involving rivers, lakes, mountains, mountain ranges and country names.

Finally, students consolidate their learning through a challenge in which they choose between a, an, the or no article across a wide variety of contexts.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to choose a, an and the accurately, recognise when no article is required and apply article rules confidently according to sound, meaning and context.

lessons.title: Word families
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore word families and learn how words can be connected through roots, prefixes, suffixes, word forms and meaning.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding what word families are
✔ Identifying common roots within groups of words
✔ Exploring how prefixes and suffixes change words
✔ Understanding morphology and how words are built
✔ Exploring roots such as struct and spect
✔ Understanding prefixes such as tri and over
✔ Sorting words into different word families
✔ Identifying odd words that do not belong in a word family
✔ Combining roots, prefixes and suffixes to form real words
✔ Recognising related nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs
✔ Exploring words ending with common suffixes such as -tion
✔ Understanding synonyms and antonyms
✔ Developing vocabulary through related words
✔ Selecting appropriate word-family members to complete sentences

Students begin by examining familiar word families such as help and write before learning how roots, prefixes and suffixes connect words through their structure and meaning. They explore examples such as triangle, tricycle and tripod to understand how the prefix tri relates to the meaning three.

The lesson then investigates the roots struct and spect. Students generate their own examples before exploring how struct is associated with building, arranging or putting things together, while spect is connected with looking and seeing.

Students practise sorting jumbled words into families including vent, cover, uni and graph, identify odd-one-out words and combine prefixes, roots and suffixes to create genuine words such as inspect, repress, invent, venture, respect, pressure, replace and placement.

The lesson then broadens the idea of related words by exploring different grammatical forms of the same root, common spelling patterns, prefixes, synonyms and antonyms. Students investigate how nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs can all belong to the same wider word family.

Finally, students apply their understanding in a sentence-completion quiz, choosing related words such as driver and driving, solve and solution, player and replay, and hurt and hurtful according to their meaning and grammatical role.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise and build word families, identify relationships between words and use their understanding of roots, prefixes, suffixes and word forms to develop their vocabulary.
